title: The finger and the moon
hookLine: a finger pointing at the moon is not the moon: words point, they are not the thing (Lankavatara)

cards: Someone stands in a dark yard, points up and says: look, the moon. And the person beside them stares hard at the end of the finger. Fingernail.
Knuckle. A little ink stain. It's a small joke, and the Lankavatara Sutra uses it to say something serious about every word of teaching, its own words included.
It's also a good way to end this week.

teach.h: A FOOL LOOKS AT THE FINGERTIP.
teach.b: Here's the picture, as the Lankavatara gives it. When someone points out the moon with a fingertip, a foolish person looks at the fingertip and not at the moon.
In the same way, the sutra says, people who cling to the letter of the teaching, to the words alone, don't see the truth the words are pointing at. Two things are true at once.

First, the finger is needed. Without someone pointing, nobody looks up. The sutra isn't telling anyone to throw words away; teachings, texts and explanations are how anyone finds the direction at all.

teach.h: THE FINGER IS NOT THE MOON.
teach.b: Second, the finger is not the moon. A person can learn every word, repeat every line, argue every point, and still be staring at a knuckle. The Lankavatara comes back to this difference between the words and the meaning.
Some later Chan and Zen teachers picked up the image too.
Now look back at this week, a week of fingers. A goddess switched bodies with Shariputra, pointing at labels that aren't fixed. Vimalakirti pointed with silence.
Then a net of jewels, a young man walking from teacher to teacher, a tower full of towers, a world in a grain.
Each one is a finger, aimed somewhere. None of them is the moon. They're there so the eyes can travel past them.
The test is small: after hearing something wise, does the attention stay on the clever words, or move on to what they were pointing at?

how: Mahayana teachers, and especially Chan and Zen teachers, use the finger and the moon to remind students that sutras and explanations point toward awakening and are not awakening itself.

o: a warning that pointing at the moon brings bad luck
a Zen joke about a student who can't see at night

games.q: someone points up at the night sky and says, look, the moon. what does the foolish person in the sutra do?
games.why: they look at the fingertip, not the moon. the sutra says those who cling to the letter of the teaching do the same.

practice: Point at the sky if you can see it, or at a lamp or a window. Look at the finger for a breath, then let your eyes move past it to what it points at, and lower the hand.
Now let the word go too, not lamp, not sky, just this light, here.

wordCard.voice: The finger and the moon. The Lankavatara's picture of words as a finger pointing: needed, but never the thing itself. Today's word.
